Jev is a filter, not an oracle. It is a zero-shot classifier with a typed interface — a framing its own CEO accepted publicly. It returns a pick, a level, or a probability; branching, retries, arithmetic, and side effects stay in your code. Every measured write-up in the field converged on the same shape: put Jev in front of the model you already use, act on its confident ends, and escalate the middle.

The corollary is the thing to internalise: the question you ask is the product. One broad question underperforms badly. A phishing task scored 62.6% as a single Jev question and 95.1% as five narrow signals recombined by a logistic regression — while a two-line regex scored 91.8%. The lift came from the decomposition, and the cheap baseline was nearly as good as the clever one. Both facts should stay uncomfortable.

The argmax is stable; the probabilities are not. 20 identical calls: choice never flipped (20/20), but the selected probability moved across a 0.11 band (sd 0.025) and a 0–3 score moved 0.18. Two thresholds within 0.11 of each other are the same threshold.

Relational questions are outside its competence, and it tells you so in the distribution. Asked nine questions over the same 119 states, per-question confidence orders cleanly by question type: literal single-state questions reach the ends (oneTimeSetupSettled 82% of items at the ends, mean confidence 0.79), while questions requiring reasoning across a goal and a file manifest do not (supersededByDurableFile 26%; neededForGoal 7% of items at the ends, never once exceeding p=0.67). Diagnostic worth reusing: run your candidate questions over one corpus and rank them by mean confidence — the ones that never leave the mid band are the ones to move into code.

Jev has no policy. This is the layer every measured write-up ended up building, and it is where the engineering lives.

The confidence gate. Act at the ends, escalate the middle, never treat 0.5 as a decision. Fit the cut-off on a few hundred of your own labelled items; a borrowed 0.9 is worth less than a small local measurement. Constrain by P4: cut-offs closer together than 0.11 are indistinguishable.

Asymmetric costs. A 0.8 that routes an email is not a 0.8 that merges a PR or spends money. Set the threshold from the cost of being wrong in that direction, not from a global default.

You don't prompt Jev. You declare the questions up front and hand it state:

choice — you give it a map of option to description (up to 255); you get back a choice (typed union of your keys) plus probabilities over every option.
score — you give it 2–10 ordered level descriptions; you get back a fractional score in [0, levels-1] plus a distribution, where score is the weighted mean.
boolean — you give it optional true/false descriptions; you get back a probability, which is P(true).

Every question in a request is evaluated in parallel against the same state, so a dozen questions costs about what one costs. Batch generously — that's the whole ergonomic win.

probabilities is optional in the spec. Jev always sends it; the LLM-adapter evaluation models legitimately don't. Code that does probabilities[choice] >= 0.9 without a null check silently starts auto-approving everything the day you swap models.

Boolean probability is P(true), not confidence. 0.5 means genuinely torn, not "unsure which way".

providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence is a separate, TypeSafe-specific statistic keyed by question id. It is not the selected option's probability and it isn't portable across providers.

One state per call. An array state is one state, not a batch. Separate states need separate calls.

Poking at TypeSafe AI's Jev — a "System One" model that returns typed decisions with probabilities instead of text — through Vercel AI Gateway and the AI SDK's experimental_evaluate.

Verified against what's actually installed here: ai@7.0.107, @ai-sdk/gateway@4.0.87, Node 25. The Gateway model id is typesafe-ai/jev (confirmed present in the models endpoint; type: "evaluation", 32K context, $0.042 / MTok input, $0 output, ZDR and no-training on all endpoints).

The question set was the defect, not the corpus. Iteration 1 asked only whether an output was intrinsically valuable — does it hold a measurement, an identifier, a decision. Nearly every tool output does, so nearly everything was kept. The question that licenses dropping is relational: has this been superseded, and does the work ahead still touch it? A successful install prints version numbers (a "finding" by the old criteria) and is pure dead weight.

Added three relational questions — supersededByDurableFile, neededForGoal, oneTimeSetupSettled — and put the forward goal plus a manifest of durable files into the state, since supersession is meaningless without knowing what already exists.

Batching is effectively free. All questions in a request evaluate in parallel against one shared state. 32 questions cost 0.91× the latency of 1 (245ms vs 269ms p50) and 2.5× the cost. Marginal ~17 input tokens per question.

You need Gateway credentials. Either one works:

Option A, an API key: works for plain node scripts, CI, anywhere. Copy .env.local.example to .env.local, then paste a key from vercel.com under AI, API Keys.

Option B, OIDC: if you'd rather not hold a key. Run vercel login, then vercel link, then vercel env pull, which writes VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN into .env.local.

Then you can run pnpm test, which is the only script that costs nothing — it runs offline, no key, no spend.

Speed and cost gains are real but an order of magnitude below the slide. Vendor: 193.6× faster, 444.6× cheaper. User-published medians: 7× speed-up (n=215) and 30× cost cut (n=180). Both can be true — the vendor compares against a frontier model writing prose with reasoning.

Where the primitives actually fit: Routing (inbox, model picker, intent, ticket desk) uses one Choice plus a Noul gate, the heaviest cluster in the field pool. Classification (spam, safety, topic, fraud) uses Choice with short labels, strong on short text but slipping on whole documents. Ranking and rubric scoring uses Score, then weights in code, reaching 91.5% agreement with a frontier model on 6,003 rubric checks. Tool selection and gating uses Choice over tools plus a Noul for safety, cutting 41% of approval prompts over 1,013 real calls with zero unsafe auto-approvals. Generation of any kind is the wrong job for it entirely — chaining Choices to emit prose is slow and bad.

Streaming conversational text UIs (like ChatGPT) have gained massive popularity over the past few months. Large language models can be extremely slow when generating long outputs compared to the latency people expect. If you build a traditional blocking UI, users might stare at a loading spinner for 5, 10, even up to 40 seconds waiting for the entire response. Streaming UIs mitigate this by displaying parts of the response as they become available, so users see the first words almost immediately instead of waiting for the whole answer.

You can use the toolChoice setting to influence when a tool is selected. It supports auto, the default, where the model can choose whether and which tools to call; required, where the model must call some tool but can pick which one; none, where the model must not call any tools; and a specific tool name, which forces the model to call that exact tool. For example, setting toolChoice to 'required' when asking about the weather in San Francisco forces the model to invoke the weather tool rather than answering from memory.

Is the Gateway hop the 3× latency gap? Same state, same questions, direct API versus Gateway. Does entropy separation hold at n=200? Ten cases is not a threshold. Does a batch contaminate itself? If rewording one option description moves answers to the other eleven questions, "fan out freely" has a hidden cost. Where is the real prunable mass in a transcript? Hypothesis: it is duplicate reads across parallel subagents, which Jev cannot see, because it evaluates one state at a time.

Swap the model, keep the code: openai.evaluationModel('gpt-5.6-luna') or anthropic.evaluationModel('claude-haiku-4.5') satisfy the same interface. Judge them against your own labeled set.
